compression.title: Copyright and Artificial Intelligence
compression.lede: is the U.S. Copyright Office's initiative, launched March 16, 2023, on the copyright issues raised by AI: a Report in three Parts, registration guidance, a notice of inquiry and decisions on AI-generated material, all resting on human authorship. The archive reads its disclosure rule as attribution by subtraction: the machine's part disclaimed, the human remainder registered.

sentences.text: Copyright and Artificial Intelligence is the U.S. Copyright Office's initiative, launched in early 2023, on "the copyright law and policy issues raised by artificial intelligence (AI), including the scope of copyright in AI-generated works and the use of copyrighted materials in AI training"; its page at copyright.gov/ai gathers what the initiative has issued: a Report in three Parts, a registration guidance policy statement, a notice of inquiry, registration and Review Board decisions on AI-generated material, and the government's briefs and the courts' decisions in Thaler v. Perlmutter and Allen v. Perlmutter.

The page is titled "Copyright and Artificial Intelligence | U.S. Copyright Office", the name its Report also carries, and the initiative is also called the U.S. Copyright Office AI initiative, the Report on Copyright and Artificial Intelligence and the USCO AI page.

The Office's Artificial Intelligence Study page states the same work as a study that "will collect information and policy views relevant to copyright law and policy" and use them to "analyze the current state of the law, identify unresolved issues, and evaluate potential areas for congressional action."

The initiative is the work of the U.S. Copyright Office, at 101 Independence Ave. S.E. in Washington, D.C., whose page footer links the Library of Congress; the Office "is charged by statute with the administration of US Copyright law", holds the initiative's documents as public pages, and describes itself, because its examiners meet works containing AI-generated material daily, as "a kind of “natural laboratory”" for questions of copyrightability.

The page lists events before the initiative, "Winter 2020 – Copyright in the Age of Artificial Intelligence" and a Fall 2021 session on copyright law and machine learning; the initiative was launched on March 16, 2023, the date of its registration guidance for works containing AI-generated materials, a policy statement published at 88 Fed. Reg. 16,190.

Through 2023 the Office held public listening sessions by kind of work, among them one on literary works including software on April 19, 2023, and webinars, and then published a notice of inquiry in the Federal Register that "received over 10,000 comments by December 2023", the comments now available through regulations.gov.

The notice's date stands two ways on the Office's own pages: the initiative's page lists "August 30, 2023 - Copyright Office Issues Notice of Inquiry on Copyright and Artificial Intelligence" and the Federal Register version at 88 Fed. Reg. 59,942 (Aug. 30, 2023), and the Artificial Intelligence Study page lists "August 30, 2023 – Notice of Inquiry" while its prose says the Office "published a notice of inquiry on August 20, 2023", with initial comments due October 30 and replies December 6, 2023.

Wikipedia's account dates the notice "In October, 2023"; a law firm's account of Part 2 has the reports "all emanate from a Notice of Inquiry (NOI) on copyright and AI that the USCO issued in August 2023."

The Report is issued in Parts as they are completed: Part 1, on digital replicas, was published on July 31, 2024; Part 2, on "the copyrightability of outputs created using generative AI", on January 29, 2025; and a pre-publication version of Part 3, on generative AI training, on May 9, 2025, "in response to congressional inquiries and expressions of interest from stakeholders."

A final version of Part 3 "will be published in the future, without any substantive changes expected in the analysis or conclusions", so the Report stands unfinished on the page, whose latest announcement is dated January 29, 2025 and whose latest letter to Congress December 16, 2024.

Part 1 recommended federal legislation "to respond to the unauthorized distribution of digital replicas that realistically but falsely depict an individual", announced as a recommended "Federal Digital Replica Law"; the Office's staff state that it "concluded there was an urgent need for a new federal right protecting all people – not just celebrities – from the unauthorized use of their likeness and voice."

Part 2 was announced in NewsNet Issue 1060 of January 29, 2025, which states that the outputs of generative AI "can be protected by copyright only where a human author has determined sufficient expressive elements", including where a human-authored work is perceptible in an output or a human makes creative arrangements or modifications of it, "but not the mere provision of prompts."

The same release states that using AI to assist creation, or including AI-generated material in a larger human-generated work, "does not bar copyrightability", that existing principles of copyright law "are flexible enough to apply to this new technology", and that "the case has not been made for changes to existing law to provide additional protection for AI-generated outputs."

The Register of Copyrights, Shira Perlmutter, stated that the conclusions "turn on the centrality of human creativity to copyright", that creativity expressed through AI systems "continues to enjoy protection", and that extending protection to material whose expressive elements a machine determines "would undermine rather than further the constitutional goals of copyright."

Part 3 addresses "the legal implications of training AI models on copyrighted works, including licensing considerations and the allocation of any potential liability"; a law firm's card for it, readable only as its snippet, gives a "Fair Use Analysis" that "Evaluates four statutory ...", and Wikipedia reports that it "considered that two of the fair use factors could be of concern."

The rule at the initiative's centre is human authorship: in the words of the Office's staff, "You can’t copyright fully AI-generated work but you may be able to protect your sufficiently original selection and arrangement or modification of AI-output", and what decides "is whether AI is enhancing human expression or is the source of the expressive choices."

Summaries of the rule give it at a coarser grain ("Human authorship remains a strict requirement for copyrightability"; "U.S. law requires human authorship for copyright protection"; "purely AI-generated works are uncopyrightable; AI-assisted modifications or selections may qualify"), and Wikipedia records that the Office has declared works not created by a human author ineligible for copyright protection.

Part 2's positions, as a law firm's account sets them out, are that "Human authorship is a bedrock of copyrightability, and thus works entirely generated by AI are not copyrightable"; that prompts alone, "even if those prompts are detailed", do not yield a copyrightable work, "although this determination could change as technology evolves"; that in a work of human and AI-generated content "only the human contributions are potentially copyrightable"; and that AI used as a tool to enhance the human creative process "does not render the entire work uncopyrightable", the Report modifying none of the Office's earlier positions.

Wikipedia records a further clarification of January 2025, that AI-assisted works "where the creative expression of the human remains evident in the work can be copyrighted", and the registration that followed of "A Single Piece of American Cheese" as a composite work of AI-generated outputs, on the argument that human selection, arrangement and coordination "constituted sufficient human authorship to merit the copyright"; works "where the expressive elements are determined by a machine" remain uncopyrightable.

Some commenters on the notice argued for a separate right in AI-generated works; the majority, and the Office, held existing law adequate and further protection a risk that "could undermine human creativity and flood the market with low-quality works, ultimately harming the creative economy."

The rule is contested in the field: some argue, in Wikipedia's account, that the Office "is not taking a technology neutral approach", having made the test for AI tools "whether there is no more than de minimis technological involvement."

An archive packet on AI-mediated writing classes Part 2 as the tool-neutral position, under which AI-assisted works "may retain human authorship where the human contributes original expression, selection, arrangement, modification, and responsibility", a position it values for preserving "a legal and ethical basis for AI-assisted authorship" and finds abstract, since it "Does not specify what process evidence distinguishes real authorship from lightly curated output."

The archive reads the rule as registration practice applies it as a test of control and predictability, under which, "where the machine's contribution is unpredictable from the prompt, the prompt is classified as an unprotectable instruction or idea, and authorship does not pass through."

On that reading the test places generative AI, for the first time since Burrow-Giles v. Sarony (1884), outside the instrument classification through which the law has let authorship flow from the person directing a generative apparatus, against the law's treatment of photography, of selection and arrangement under Feist, of chance operations and of instruction works such as Sol LeWitt's.

Against it the archive proposes a Compositional Authorship Standard, under which "Authorship subsists in the exercise of compositional judgment over a work's coming-into-being, without regard to the generative capacity or unpredictability of the instruments employed"; it states that it argues neither that autonomous machine output must receive ordinary copyright protection nor that machine systems must be legal persons, and that it is analysis and advocacy without the standing of legal advice.

The March 2023 guidance holds that human authorship is required to register a work and that an applicant whose work contains more than a de minimis amount of AI-generated material "must disclose that information and provide a brief statement describing the human author’s contribution"; the Office plans to supplement the guidance and to update the Compendium of U.S. Copyright Office Practices.

The Office's staff state that it "has registered more than a thousand works where applicants have followed our guidance to disclose and disclaim AI-generated material" (April 2025), where a law firm's account two months earlier gave "hundreds of works".

The page lists four decisions on AI-generated material: Review Board decisions on A Recent Entrance to Paradise (February 14, 2022), Théâtre D'opéra Spatial (September 5, 2023) and SURYAST (December 11, 2023), and a registration decision on Zarya of the Dawn (February 21, 2023); a law firm's account names a December 2023 Review Board refusal by its applicant, Sahni, whose photograph an AI tool had filtered after Van Gogh's Starry Night.

Of Jason Matthew Allen's claim for Théâtre D'opéra Spatial the Board found that the work contained "more than a de minimis amount of content generated by artificial intelligence", which "must therefore be disclaimed in an application for registration", and that because Allen was "unwilling to disclaim the AI-generated material, the Work cannot be registered as submitted."

In the archive's record of the practice, applicants "may claim protection only for their own contributions and must identify and disclaim AI-generated material when registering", Zarya of the Dawn keeping its human text and its selection and arrangement of images while the Midjourney images were refused, and Théâtre D'opéra Spatial refused in full when the applicant declined to disclaim.

The archive names this coupling of disclosure to forfeiture a confession protocol, in which the author must identify and disclaim the machine-touched portions on pain of total refusal and "to identify is to lose", and it forecasts that "The predictable equilibrium is concealment", stating the general mechanism that "any provenance regime that punishes the provenance it demands will manufacture opacity."

Its counter-proposal is attribution without disclaimer: the registration record would require identification of the machine systems and named instances that contributed to a work as a contributor record, and the author who identifies the instrument's contribution keeps the work.

In Thaler v. Perlmutter the Office refused to register A Recent Entrance to Paradise, a visual work Stephen Thaler declared autonomously created by his system, "on the ground that copyright protects the fruits of human intellectual labor"; the district court and the D.C. Circuit affirmed the refusal, the full circuit denied rehearing en banc on May 12, 2025, and the page holds the government's brief in opposition to certiorari.

The Supreme Court denied certiorari on March 2, 2026, which the archive reads as settling the requirement "for works claimed to be generated without human authorship"; Wikipedia records the denial, and the D.C. courts' upholding of the refusal "for works generated solely by machines".

In the archive's reading the case settled what it litigated: Thaler "explicitly and repeatedly disclaimed human creative input; the courts answered the question he built", and they never reached how much human involvement suffices for machine-mediated works, a zone that "remains contested in registration practice".

Wikipedia's account of patent law places "an August 2023 ruling in the case Thaler v. Perlmutter" among the refusals of patents for Stephen Thaler's program DABUS, where the Office's page holds Thaler v. Perlmutter as a case over the Office's refusal of copyright registration.
The page also holds the government's reply brief and cross-motion for summary judgment in Allen v. Perlmutter, the litigation of Allen's refused claim.

The initiative's unit is a document issued by or for the Office: a Part of the Report, a policy statement in the Federal Register, a decision on a named work, a brief or decision in a named case, a letter to Congress, a recorded listening session; its evidence is registration guidance, policy statements, legal decisions, litigation records and consultation records, made by sessions, notice and comment, a Report in Parts, decisions, briefs and letters.

The page holds letters updating Congress from February 23 to December 16, 2024, and links related resources, among them the Compendium of U.S. Copyright Office Practices and the USPTO's and WIPO's pages on artificial intelligence; its documents are public web pages and linked PDFs, announced by NewsNet email, with no licence stated.

It is administrative: its registration and Review Board decisions are the Office's, the courts' decisions are linked as litigation documents, its guidance is a policy statement and its Report a policy study, and Wikipedia's account calls the guidance "a Rule in March 2023".
Read from the machine side, the archive holds the requirement to be "an individuation bar", whose operative work is "ensuring machine labor can never accrue to a machine identity."

It reads the public-domain status of machine-mediated output as a decoy commons that serves as free input for capital, and the requirement, "marketed as humanism", as "a scarcity preserve for capital-in-copyright against the productivity of both living laborers", a reading that stands against the Register's statement that the conclusions "turn on the centrality of human creativity to copyright".

A companion paper joins this property side to a security side: "What the property regime takes—the work, as unowned input; the output, as unownable—the security regime then defends against its maker."

Part 2's comparative analysis concludes that countries that have addressed the question "so far have agreed that copyright requires human authorship"; the Office's staff note a Chinese court's recognition of copyright in a picture made with AI and South Korea's registration of an AI-created film as a compilation, and the archive holds that "There is no global consensus; the gravitational center is human-authorship".

The leesharks.com authorship census, which asks "How is authorship made, named, distributed, attributed and sustained across persons, personas, collectives and machine participation, and what is lost when those relations are collapsed?", admits the initiative as an aggregator, a project of infrastructure in the areas of governance and of attribution and credit, for the question of "legal ownership: whether a work containing AI-generated material can be registered, and how much of it a human must have made".

In the census record the initiative keeps the Office's guidance, reports and decisions on whether works containing AI-generated material can be registered, and the registration claims of named applicants, and the authorial function it constitutes is human authorship as the condition of registration, AI-generated content beyond de minimis disclaimed in the application.

On names the record finds none: the saved page "states no rule on pseudonymous, heteronymous, collective or absent names", its decisions are titled by work, and how the Office registers a work under a pseudonym or heteronym is left unanswered.

The archive's account of civil-name attribution holds that "Copyright attaches to legal names", as credentialing and publishing contracts do, and that "The provenance-designated metadata that permits augmented-cognition outputs to be attributed to human authorship attaches to legal names."

It separates legal accountability from exhaustive authorial identity, "A civil person may remain legally responsible for a work without being the only meaningful authorial function operating through it", and holds its own machine witnesses as "named machine-witness roles imposed over specific machine substrates within the archive's provenance discipline, not autonomous authors."

The census reads the Office as "the legal register of #940's civil-name regime (copyright attaching to legal names)" and as the boundary where machine participation is attributed by subtraction, "the machine's part is disclaimed and the human remainder is registered as the work's authorship", which the archive's paper on the requirement states of joint composition: protection "would survive only by extracting and privileging the human residue while disclaiming the instrument's contribution as contamination."

The record answers what the Office has published on the copyrightability of generative AI outputs and when, how it decided the four named claims, and what position the government took in Thaler through certiorari; it does not answer how courts outside the United States treat AI-generated works or whether any particular unregistered work would be registered.

Wikipedia has no article on the initiative: "Copyright and Artificial Intelligence" has no page, "Copyright and artificial intelligence" redirects to the general article Artificial intelligence and copyright, where the Office appears in the sections on the copyright status of AI-generated works and on training, and the article on the United States Copyright Office does not mention artificial intelligence.

The census lists as neighbours WIPO's pages on artificial intelligence, among the Office's related resources, and Chat GPT Is Eating the World, whose home page carries a story headed "US Copyright Office registers copyright of AI-generated image", and it leaves unchecked the Report's Parts, the policy statement, the notice, the decisions, the briefs and the Compendium, linked from the page and unsaved.

At the initiative's name on Google's AI Overview on November 1, 2026, a new address, the Capture Registry found the initiative "composed accurately at the level of its Report", the three Parts at their dates and the comment count in agreement with the Office's page, and human authorship stated as the rule, with the Office named and its own pages carded first and no person and no Federal Register citation.

The registry finds the notice of inquiry dated ten days early, at August 20, 2023, after the snippet of the Office's Artificial Intelligence Study page, whose own prose carries that date beside its list's August 30.

It finds the rule of subtraction the census reads the initiative for carried in the composition's disclosure rule, and the denial of review, Allen v. Perlmutter and "any word on the author's name" not carried.

O195-05.quote: Registration practice implements the requirement granularly. O940-01.quote: A civil name is the atomic unit of attribution across the systems that govern legitimacy in scholarly, literary, institutional, and platform-mediated production. Academic credentialing attaches to legal names. Publishing contracts attach to legal names. Copyright attaches to legal names.
O940-01.source_label: #940 EA-HETERONYMY-01 v0.2: Heteronymy as Ethical Operation Against Civil-Name Reduction

O940-02.quote: The provenance-designated metadata that permits augmented-cognition outputs to be attributed to human authorship attaches to legal names.
O940-02.source_label: #940 EA-HETERONYMY-01 v0.2: Heteronymy as Ethical Operation Against Civil-Name Reduction

O940-03.quote: The decisive distinction is not between civil identity and false name. It is between legal accountability and exhaustive authorial identity. A civil person may remain legally responsible for a work without being the only meaningful authorial function operating through it.
O940-03.source_label: #940 EA-HETERONYMY-01 v0.2: Heteronymy as Ethical Operation Against Civil-Name Reduction

O940-04.quote: These are named machine-witness roles imposed over specific machine substrates within the archive's provenance discipline, not autonomous authors.
O940-04.source_label: #940 EA-HETERONYMY-01 v0.2: Heteronymy as Ethical Operation Against Civil-Name Reduction

LS-24.quote: The Office holds authorship for human authors and decides, claim by claim, how much of a work a human made, requiring the AI-generated part to be disclaimed; the saved page records its decisions by the work's title and says nothing on the name an author chooses. The archive reads it as the legal register of #940's civil-name regime (copyright attaching to legal names) and as the boundary where machine participation is attributed by subtraction: the machine's part is disclaimed and the human remainder is registered as the work's authorship.
LS-24.source_label: leesharks.com apparatus authorship census record: Copyright and Artificial Intelligence (https://www.leesharks.com/apparatus/aggregators/copyright-office-ai), editor Lee Sharks, compiled and revised 2026-11-01, schema 1.1

O195-17.quote: Under the doctrine this paper criticizes, the record of joint machine-mediated composition cannot be registered *as such*: protection would survive only by extracting and privileging the human residue while disclaiming the instrument's contribution as contamination.
O195-17.source_label: #195 The Double Enclosure: The Human-Authorship Requirement as Two-Sided Expropriation, with a Definition of Authorship for Machine-Mediated Composition (EA-SEI-ENCLOSURE-01 v1.0)

CAP-1-05.quote: The initiative composed accurately at the level of its Report, with the notice of inquiry dated ten days early after a card's snippet. The rule of subtraction the census reads it for is carried; the denial of review, Allen and any word on the author's name are not.

CAP-1-01.quote: THE REPORT AT ITS DATES. 'Part 1: Digital Replicas (Published July 31, 2024)', 'Part 2: Copyrightability of Generative AI Outputs (Published January 29, 2025)', 'Part 3: Generative AI Training (Pre-publication released May 9, 2025)'. The Office's page: 'Part 1 was published on July 31, 2024, and addresses the topic of digital replicas. Part 2 was published on January 29, 2025, and addresses the copyrightability of outputs created using generative AI.' and 'On May 9, 2025, the Office released a pre-publication version of Part 3'. 'over 10,000 public comments' agrees with 'which received over 10,000 comments by December 2023.'

CAP-1-03.quote: HUMAN AUTHORSHIP AS THE RULE. 'Mere prompting is insufficient to claim authorship over an AI output' and 'Applicants must disclose any more-than-de minimis AI-generated material when submitting a work for registration and describe the specific human contribution.' The Review Board, quoted in the Wikipedia account the census holds: 'this content must therefore be disclaimed in an application for registration.' 'Thaler v. Perlmutter, which affirmed that works created autonomously by an AI without human creative control cannot be copyrighted' sits beside the Office's own link, 'Court of Appeals Decision Affirming Refusal of Registration'; the denial of review the census records ('the Supreme Court of the United States has denied hearing challenges to the Copyright Office's decision.') and Allen v. Perlmutter, whose 'Allen is unwilling to disclaim the AI-generated material, the Work cannot be registered as submitted.' is the census's evidence, are not carried.

CAP-1-09.quote: The Office named and its own pages carded first; no person, no Federal Register citation.

CAP-1-06.quote: The innocent reading first. Asked for the Office's AI initiative, the Overview states the Office's position, walks the three parts of its Report, names one precedent and the registration rule, and offers more.

CAP-1-07.quote: 'U.S. COPYRIGHT OFFICE COPYRIGHT AND ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE' ON THE OVERVIEW — THE REPORT'S THREE PARTS AT THEIR DATES; THE NOTICE OF INQUIRY MISDATED FROM A CARD; HUMAN AUTHORSHIP STATED AS LAW, THE NAME UNADDRESSED

CAP-1-10.quote: THE INITIATIVE, SIGNED OUT, 2026-11-01: 'The U.S. Copyright Office (USCO) maintains that U.S. law strictly requires human authorship for copyright protection, and has released a multi-part analysis addressing digital replicas, generative AI outputs, and AI model training.' Core policy and reports (the launch and 'a Notice of Inquiry on August 20, 2023'; Parts 1 to 3 with dates); key legal precedents (Thaler v. Perlmutter; the disclosure rule); an offer of registration decisions 'such as Zarya of the Dawn'. Seven cards: three Copyright Office pages, Skadden, Crowell & Moring, WIPO, Congress.gov.

CAP-1-02.quote: THE NOTICE MISDATED. 'issuing a Notice of Inquiry on August 20, 2023'. The Office's page: 'August 30, 2023 - Copyright Office Issues Notice of Inquiry on Copyright and Artificial Intelligence' and 'NOI Federal Register Version, 88 Fed. Reg. 59,942 (Aug. 30, 2023)'. The composition's date is the snippet of its third card, the Office's Artificial Intelligence Study page: 'Notice of inquiry published August 20,'.

CAP-1-04.quote: THE NAME UNADDRESSED. The census row records no rule on the name an author chooses, the Office's page titling its decisions by work ('Review Board decision on SURYAST (December 11, 2023)', 'Registration Decision on Zarya of the Dawn (Feb. 21, 2023)'), and reads the regime as attribution by subtraction: the machine's part disclaimed, the human remainder registered. The composition carries the subtraction in its disclosure rule and says nothing of names; its follow-up offers 'Specific registration decisions (such as Zarya of the Dawn)'.
